questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes what a base does?

options.text: It neutralises an acid, forming a salt and water
options.explanation: That reaction is the defining job of a base, whether or not the base dissolves.

options.text: It dissolves in water to give hydroxide ions only
options.explanation: Dissolving to give hydroxide ions describes an alkali, a subset of bases only.
options.misconception: alkali definition applied to every base

options.text: It reacts with a salt to form an acid
options.explanation: The reactants and products are reversed here; acids and bases make salts, not the other way round.

options.text: It turns blue litmus paper red
options.explanation: That is acid behaviour; bases turn red litmus paper blue instead.

questions.stem: Copper(II) oxide is insoluble in water. How should it be classified?

options.text: A base, but not an alkali
options.explanation: It neutralises acids, which makes it a base, but it cannot dissolve, so it is not an alkali.

options.text: An alkali, because metal oxides are always alkaline
options.explanation: The oxide family name does not decide solubility; this oxide stays solid, so the alkali label fails.

options.text: Neither, because only hydroxides can be bases
options.explanation: Oxides, hydroxides and carbonates of metals all act as bases, so copper(II) oxide qualifies.

options.text: An alkali, because it neutralises acids quickly
options.explanation: Speed of reaction has nothing to do with the alkali label, which is about dissolving in water.

questions.stem: A solution has pH 11. What does this show about it?

options.text: It is alkaline, so the dissolved substance is an alkali
options.explanation: Values above 7 are alkaline, and the soluble base responsible is an alkali.

options.text: It is a strong acid
options.explanation: The pH direction has been reversed; acids sit below 7, not above it.

options.text: It is pure water
options.explanation: Pure water sits at pH 7; a value of 11 is far from neutral.

options.text: Its pH says nothing about whether it is an alkali
options.explanation: The pH scale exists precisely to report acidity and alkalinity, and 11 reports alkaline.

questions.stem: What is present in every aqueous alkali that makes the solution alkaline?

options.text: Hydroxide ions
options.explanation: The hydroxide ion is what makes an aqueous solution an alkali, whatever the parent base.

options.text: Ammonium ions
options.explanation: Ammonium ions appear only in the ammonia case, not in every alkaline solution.
options.misconception: ammonia case generalised to all alkalis

options.text: Oxide ions
options.explanation: Oxide ions belong to solid metal oxides; in water the hydroxide ion is the marker.

options.text: Hydrogen ions
options.explanation: Hydrogen ions make solutions acidic, the exact opposite of the target.

questions.stem: Ammonia solution acts as a base. Why is it described as unusual?

options.text: It is a compound of nitrogen, not a metal oxide or hydroxide
options.explanation: Nearly every base on the course is a metal oxide, hydroxide or carbonate, so the nitrogen compound stands out.

options.text: It is the only base that neutralises acids
options.explanation: Every base neutralises acids; that is the family definition, not a special property of ammonia.

options.text: It produces hydrogen ions instead of hydroxide ions in water
options.explanation: Ammonia reacts with water to produce hydroxide ions, which is exactly why it is alkaline.

options.text: It is the only base that dissolves completely in water
options.explanation: Sodium and potassium hydroxide also dissolve freely, so exclusivity is false.

questions.stem: State the products formed when an acid reacts with a base.
questions.modelAnswer: A neutralisation reaction between an acid and a base gives a salt and water.

questions.stem: State the pH values that identify an alkali.
questions.modelAnswer: An alkali has a pH above 7 (any value greater than 7).

questions.stem: Explain why copper(II) oxide is a base but is not an alkali.
questions.modelAnswer: Copper(II) oxide neutralises acids, so it is a base, but it does not dissolve in water, so it cannot be an alkali; every alkali is a soluble base while many bases never dissolve.

questions.stem: A colourless solution turns red litmus paper blue. State what class of substance it is and one pH value it could have.
questions.modelAnswer: It is basic (alkaline) - an alkali or soluble base - with a pH above 7, such as pH 11.

questions.stem: Which ions does aqueous potassium hydroxide contain?

options.text: K+ and OH-
options.explanation: Potassium hydroxide splits into potassium ions and hydroxide ions in water.

options.text: K+ and O2-
options.explanation: The oxide ion belongs to solid oxides; in solution the hydroxide ion carries the alkalinity.

options.text: K2+ and OH-
options.explanation: Potassium is group 1 and forms only 1+ ions, so K2+ is not a real species here.

options.text: K+ and H+
options.explanation: Hydrogen ions would make the solution acidic, not alkaline.

questions.stem: Ammonia gas dissolves in water. Which ions appear in the solution?

options.text: NH4+ and OH-
options.explanation: The gas reacts with water to give ammonium ions and hydroxide ions.

options.text: NH3 and OH-
options.explanation: NH3 is the neutral gas molecule, not an ion in the solution.
options.misconception: neutral molecule listed as an ion

options.text: NH4+ and H+
options.explanation: Hydrogen ions would make an acidic solution, but ammonia solution is alkaline.

options.text: N3- and OH-
options.explanation: Nitride ions do not survive in water; the nitrogen appears as ammonium instead.

questions.stem: Why must the words ammonia and ammonium not be used interchangeably?

options.text: Ammonia names the gas NH3 while ammonium names the ion NH4+
options.explanation: The gas and the ion are different species, so the names name different things.

options.text: They describe different concentrations of the same solution
options.explanation: The words separate chemical species, not strengths of one solution.

options.text: Ammonium is the unreactive form of ammonia
options.explanation: The ammonium ion takes part in its own chemistry; reactivity is not what separates the words.

options.text: Ammonia is an ion and ammonium is a compound
options.explanation: Both halves of the statement are swapped; ammonia is the gas and ammonium is the ion.

questions.stem: A student tests two clear solutions and both turn red litmus paper blue. What can be concluded?

options.text: Both solutions contain hydroxide ions
options.explanation: Alkaline solutions carry hydroxide ions, and that is the only safe shared conclusion.

options.text: Both must be sodium hydroxide
options.explanation: Any alkali turns the paper blue, so the parent base cannot be fixed from this test alone.

options.text: Neither can contain ammonia
options.explanation: Ammonia solution is alkaline and would give exactly this result.

options.text: Both are definitely soluble metal hydroxides
options.explanation: Aqueous ammonia is a counter-example, so the claim is too strong.

questions.stem: Which row pairs the alkali with the ions it forms in water?

options.text: Sodium hydroxide gives Na+ and OH-
options.explanation: That is the correct split for sodium hydroxide in water.

options.text: Potassium hydroxide gives K+ and O2-
options.explanation: The hydroxide ion, not the oxide ion, appears when an alkali dissolves.
options.misconception: oxide slip in the ion table

options.text: Aqueous ammonia gives NH3 and OH-
options.explanation: NH3 is the dissolved gas molecule; the ion present is NH4+.
options.misconception: gas molecule listed among the ions

options.text: Sodium hydroxide gives NaOH2- and H+
options.explanation: Neither of those species exists in this solution; sodium and hydroxide ions do.

questions.stem: Name the two ions present in a solution of sodium hydroxide.
questions.modelAnswer: Sodium hydroxide solution contains sodium ions (Na+) and hydroxide ions (OH-).

questions.stem: Name the two ions present in aqueous ammonia and state how they come to exist.
questions.modelAnswer: Aqueous ammonia contains ammonium ions (NH4+) and hydroxide ions (OH-), formed when ammonia reacts with the water.

questions.stem: Explain why the words ammonia and ammonium must not be confused with each other.
questions.modelAnswer: Ammonia is the neutral gas NH3, while ammonium is the positive ion NH4+ that exists in solution; one is a gas and the other an ion, and their formulas differ by one hydrogen.

questions.stem: A student adds sodium hydroxide dropwise to dilute hydrochloric acid. Explain why the mixture can pass from turning litmus red to turning litmus blue.
questions.modelAnswer: The added alkali first neutralises the acid; once every H+ has reacted, spare hydroxide ions remain in solution, so the mixture becomes alkaline and turns red litmus blue.
